newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong to publish civil liberties amendments.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong to publish civil liberties amendments.

text.p: Controversial changes to Hong Kong's civil liberties laws will be published and submitted to the territory's China-appointed interim legislature this week, an advisor to future leader Tung Chee-hwa said on Tuesday.

The proposed amendments, expected to restrict demonstrations and ban overseas funding of political parties, have drawn a storm of protest from Hong Kong's active pro-democracy lobby and the outgoing colonial administration.
The democracy lobby plans to launch a legal challenge to any laws passed by the Beijing-installed Provisional Legislature, arguing the body itself is unconstitutional.

Tam Yiu-chung, a member of Tung's Executive Council, said he was confident any challenge would fail and that the proposals would be published in Hong Kong on Thursday and submitted to the provisional legislature on Saturday as planned.
Tam spoke to reporters after attending a meeting of the council, where the details of the amendments were debated.
The provisional legislature, selected in December, meets across the border in the Chinese city of Shenzhen to avoid triggering any legal action for operating in Hong Kong.
It will replace the existing elected legislature when Hong Kong, a British colony for more than 150 years, reverts to China at midnight on June 30.

Tung's aides have said the incoming government is looking to soften but not scrap some of the original amendment proposals following a three-week public consultation exercise that yielded more than 6,000 submissions.
Local newspapers speculated that Tung's administration may relax the notice period for demonstrations and redefine political parties to ensure that religious and labour organisations are excluded.
A Tung spokesman declined to comment on specifics.
Concessions are unlikely to mollify pro-democracy activists who have lobbied against the amendments, angering Tung who accused them of "badmouthing" Hong Kong.
A handful of activists, who staged a protest outside Tung's office on Tuesday, attacked reports of compromise as a "sugar-coated poison-pill".
The middle-of-the-road Ming Pao newspaper said there was no need to tighten Hong Kong's existing ordinances.
The sentencing on Monday of three activists for storming the Japanese consulate last October showed the legal system was sufficient to control demonstrations, the newspaper said.
"It had struck a balance between the freedom of assembly and social stability," it said.

The three activists, members of a Hong Kong pressure group protesting against the landing by Japanese right-wingers on a chain of uninhabited islands claimed by Beijing, Tokyo and Taipei, were fined and ordered to pay costs.

Tung has said the amendments were needed to prevent a repeat of such lawlessness, argued they were no more onerous than those in some Western countries and merely returned Hong Kong laws to where they were before the 1991 Bill of Rights ordinance.

Singapore's elder statesman, Lee Kuan Yew, urged Tung in an interview with the Financial Times on Tuesday to scrap all political reforms instigated by Governor Chris Patten to win the confidence of the Chinese leadership.
Patten's democratic reforms angered China, which responded by drawing up plans to install the interim provisional legislature for a year until new elections are held.
